value.overview: The Cinnamon Becard (Pachyramphus cinnamomeus) is a small, compact passerine of the becard family, Tityridae. It is named for its warm cinnamon, rufous, and buff plumage, and males and females are generally alike. The species inhabits humid tropical forests, forest borders, secondary woodland, and clearings from southern Mexico through Central America to parts of northern South America. It is usually detected by its soft, plaintive, whistled song or by brief sallies from a shaded perch.
value.classification: The Cinnamon Becard belongs to the family Tityridae, which includes becards, tityras, and related species. Its scientific name is Pachyramphus cinnamomeus.
value.identification: This becard is about 14–15 cm long and has a dark bill, dark eye, and dark gray legs. The crown and upperparts are rich cinnamon-rufous to tawny, while the underparts are buff, ochraceous, or cinnamon-buff, usually becoming paler on the throat and belly. The wings and tail are also rufous. It can be confused with other brown forest birds, but its uniformly warm coloration, compact becard shape, and plaintive, reedy song are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Cinnamon Becard ranges from southern Mexico through most of Central America, except El Salvador, and south to Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela. In Costa Rica it occurs on both slopes, but is more frequent on the Caribbean side and generally less common on the Pacific slope. It uses humid evergreen forest, forest interior and edges, secondary growth, shaded clearings, and sometimes scattered trees near cultivated areas. In Costa Rica it is mainly a lowland and foothill bird, with records extending into lower elevations of the Cordilleras.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica, where it is not regarded as a regular long-distance migrant. Limited local or seasonal movements may occur, especially in parts of the northern range.
value.breeding: The breeding season is incompletely known, but in Costa Rica it includes approximately March through July. The nest is a bulky, roughly spherical structure with a side entrance, made from dead leaves, fibers, moss, rootlets, and other plant material. It is usually placed in a branch fork, often high in the canopy, although lower placements have been recorded. Nests may occur near active wasp nests. Clutches generally contain three or four eggs; the female incubates, while both parents feed the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Cinnamon Becard eats mainly insects and other arthropods, supplemented by berries and other small fruits. It usually forages alone or in pairs from the middle levels of forest to the canopy. A bird often remains motionless on a perch while inspecting nearby foliage, then makes a short sally to glean prey from leaves or twigs. It sometimes joins mixed-species feeding flocks and may take insects from open vegetation or scattered trees.
value.behavior: This is a quiet, inconspicuous becard that often remains hidden among leafy branches. It commonly occurs singly or in pairs and may join small mixed-species groups outside periods of strong territorial activity. Its flight between perches is usually short and direct. The song is a thin, mellow, plaintive series of whistles or rapidly repeated musical notes, often given from the canopy or upper middle levels of forest. Its secretive habits can make it easier to hear than see.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although it remains widespread and is not currently regarded as threatened.
